title: WHEN LOVE TURNS INTO CONTEMPT: THE TERRIFYING LESSON CHRISTIAN MARRIAGES MUST LEARN FROM DAVID AND MICHAL
paragraphs:
WHEN LOVE TURNS INTO CONTEMPT: THE TERRIFYING LESSON CHRISTIAN MARRIAGES MUST LEARN FROM DAVID AND MICHAL
She once loved David enough to risk her life for him. Years later, she looked through a window, watched the same man worship God, and despised him in her heart. What happened between those two moments should make every Christian husband and wife examine what is quietly happening inside their own home.
There is a sentence in the Bible that can haunt a marriage if you understand what it is saying.
Not because somebody committed adultery in that particular scene.
Not because divorce papers were lying on a table.
Not because anyone announced that the marriage was over.
The marriage was still there.
The husband was still the husband.
The wife was still the wife.
The house was still standing.
But something inside the relationship had become terribly sick.
Scripture says:
“And as the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart.”
—2 Samuel 6:16
Read that last phrase again.
“She despised him in her heart.”
The Hebrew is devastating.
וַתִּבֶז לוֹ בְּלִבָּהּ
vat·tivez lo belibbāh
The verb comes from בָּזָה (bāzâ)—to despise, disdain, regard with contempt.
And בְּלִבָּהּ (belibbāh) means “in her heart.”
Before the contempt came out of Michal’s mouth, it was already living inside her.
That is where some marriages begin dying.
Not in the courtroom.
Not with packed suitcases.
Not even necessarily with screaming.
Sometimes a marriage begins bleeding silently when one spouse starts looking at the other and thinking…
“I don’t respect you anymore.”
And perhaps that sentence makes you uncomfortable because you know exactly what it feels like to sleep beside someone while carrying resentment you have never surrendered to God.
You still attend church together.
You still upload the anniversary picture.
You still call each other “husband” and “wife.”
People still say, “What a beautiful Christian family.”
But strangers see the photograph.
God sees the heart.
And there may be years of disappointment sitting between two people who once could not imagine life apart.
That is why the story of David and Michal deserves far more than a shallow sermon about a dancing king and an irritated wife.
This marriage had history.
Painful history.
Complicated history.
And Scripture refuses to make that history as simple as “David good, Michal bad.”
Long before Michal despised David, Michal loved David.
That detail matters.
First Samuel 18:20 says:
“And Michal Saul's daughter loved David.”
Later, Scripture repeats that Saul knew “that Michal Saul's daughter loved him” (1 Samuel 18:28).
This woman was not introduced to us as someone who hated David.
She loved him.

And when Saul later plotted to kill David, Michal helped save her husband’s life. First Samuel 19 records that she warned David that he would be killed if he did not escape, lowered him through a window, and helped him flee.
Notice the painful irony.
In 1 Samuel 19, Michal is associated with a window while helping David escape death.
In 2 Samuel 6, Michal is again at a window—but now she is watching him with contempt.
Same woman.
Same man.
Different heart.
What happened in between?
Life happened.
Power happened.
Separation happened.
Family conflict happened.
Other marriages happened.
Political decisions happened.
Wounds accumulated.

While David was fleeing Saul, Michal was given to another man, Palti or Paltiel (1 Samuel 25:44). Later, after Saul’s death, David demanded Michal’s return as part of negotiations surrounding his kingship (2 Samuel 3:13–16).
And Scripture gives us one of those heartbreaking details that is easy to rush past.
Her second husband followed behind her weeping.
Then Abner ordered him to go home.
The Bible does not tell us everything Michal felt through all of this, so we should not pretend that it does.
We cannot diagnose her heart beyond what Scripture reveals.
But we can say what the text plainly shows: Michal’s life and marriage had passed through extraordinary upheaval.
And David himself was not a flawless husband.
That matters too.
The Bible does not invite husbands to read this story, point at Michal, and announce, “See? My wife needs to respect me.”

David had multiple wives. His household would later experience devastating consequences connected to his own sins and failures. His later adultery with Bathsheba and orchestration of Uriah’s death are condemned unmistakably by Scripture (2 Samuel 11–12).
David was capable of extraordinary worship.
David was also capable of catastrophic sin.
That is precisely why this story is so painfully human.
Because Christian marriage is not the union of two perfect people.
It is the covenant union of two sinners who desperately need the grace of God.
And maybe that is where this story enters your house.
Maybe your spouse is not the person you thought you married.
Or perhaps the more uncomfortable truth is that you are not the person your spouse thought they married.
Maybe years ago she admired you.
Now she mostly notices what you failed to become.
Maybe years ago he listened when you spoke.
Now his eyes barely leave the phone.
Maybe there was once affection in the bedroom, laughter in the kitchen, prayer beside the bed, ridiculous private jokes nobody else understood.
Now conversations sound like transactions.
“Did you pay that?”
“Pick up the children.”
“What time are you coming home?”
“Did you remember?”
“Goodnight.”
And underneath all of it sits something neither person wants to name.
Contempt.
It is possible to remain married while emotionally standing at the window.
Watching.
Judging.
Keeping score.
Remembering every failure.
Interpreting everything through accumulated disappointment.
That is approximately where we find Michal when David brings the ark of the covenant into Jerusalem.
David is celebrating before the LORD.
Second Samuel 6:14 says:
“David danced before the LORD with all his might.”
The Hebrew says:
וְדָוִד מְכַרְכֵּר בְּכָל־עֹז לִפְנֵי יְהוָה
veDavid mekharker bekhol-oz lifnei YHWH.
David is celebrating with extraordinary energy “before the LORD”—לִפְנֵי יְהוָה (lifnei YHWH).
That phrase matters because David later explains his motivation.
When Michal confronts him sarcastically about how “glorious” the king had made himself by exposing himself before the servant women, David answers:
“It was before the LORD…”
—2 Samuel 6:21
David understood his celebration primarily as worship directed toward God.
But Michal saw something else.
She saw embarrassment.
She saw impropriety.
She saw a king behaving beneath the dignity she believed his position demanded.
And when David finally returned home “to bless his household” (2 Samuel 6:20), he walked straight into a confrontation.
Think about that.
He comes home intending to bless.
He receives contempt.
Michal says sarcastically:
“How glorious was the king of Israel to day…”
The words sound complimentary.
They are anything but.
And married people know this language.
“Oh, wonderful.”
“You’re such a great husband.”
“Mother of the year.”
“Of course you forgot.”
“Look who finally decided to come home.”
Sometimes the vocabulary sounds ordinary while the tone carries a knife.

But David’s response should not automatically be treated as a model of gentle marital conflict resolution either. He defends his worship and invokes God’s choice of him over Michal’s father and household.
The exchange becomes painful.
She attacks.
He answers.
Old family history enters the room.
And suddenly this is bigger than dancing.
That happens in marriages every day.
The argument is supposedly about dishes.
But it is not about dishes.
It is supposedly about money.
But it is not only about money.
It is supposedly about coming home late.
But underneath that argument is:
“You don't value me.”
“You don't see me.”
“You embarrassed me.”
“I cannot trust you.”
“You never changed.”
“I feel alone.”
“You remind me of what hurt me.”
And two people begin fighting tonight with ammunition collected over ten years.
This is why Christians must be careful with 2 Samuel 6:23:
“Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death.”

Some interpreters connect her childlessness directly with the preceding confrontation; others caution that the verse itself does not explicitly explain the biological or providential mechanism. We should therefore resist inventing details God did not reveal.
But the narrative ending is intentionally bleak.
A relationship that once contained love and courageous loyalty ends its biblical portrait with distance, contempt, conflict, and barrenness.
And there is a warning here that Christian marriages desperately need.
Be careful what you allow to live untreated in your heart.
Because contempt rarely arrives overnight.
It grows.
One unresolved wound.
Another disappointment.
Another apology never given.
Another promise broken.
Another comparison.
Another cruel joke.
Another night going to bed angry.
Another month without meaningful conversation.
Another year pretending everything is fine.
Until eventually you stop seeing your spouse as someone to love and begin seeing them as someone to prosecute.
Every mistake becomes evidence.
Every weakness becomes a weapon.
Every disagreement becomes another trial.
And you become both attorney and judge.
But here is where this article cannot end with David and Michal.
Because David cannot save your marriage.
Michal cannot save your marriage.
Marriage advice cannot save your soul.
Jesus Christ must remain at the center.
And Jesus takes contempt seriously because He takes the heart seriously.
In Matthew 5:21–22, Christ goes beneath the external act of murder and confronts sinful anger and contempt within the human heart.
Jesus does not merely ask what your hands have done.
He exposes what your heart has become.
That means you can be sexually faithful to your spouse and still need to repent of how you treat them.
You can never have committed adultery and still murder intimacy through humiliation.
You can quote Scripture and use it as ammunition.
You can demand “submission” while refusing sacrificial love.
You can demand “love” while refusing respect.
You can win theological arguments while destroying the person sitting across from you.
Christian husband, Ephesians 5 does not give you permission to become a domestic dictator.
It tells husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
—Ephesians 5:25
The standard is Christ.
Sacrifice.
Self-giving love.

And Christian wife, biblical respect is not permission for sin, abuse, manipulation, or evil to remain unchallenged. Scripture never requires someone to participate in wickedness. But neither does hurt give any Christian permission to cultivate contempt as a permanent residence of the heart.
Both husband and wife stand beneath the lordship of Jesus.
Both need grace.
Both need repentance.
Both need truth.
And sometimes one spouse may repent before the other does.
Sometimes reconciliation requires difficult conversations.
Sometimes pastoral help is needed.
Sometimes professional Christian counseling can help uncover patterns a couple can no longer see for themselves.

And where abuse, coercion, violence, or credible danger exists, “just submit more” is not responsible biblical counsel. Safety, truthful disclosure, appropriate authorities, and wise pastoral and professional support may be necessary. Forgiveness does not mean pretending evil is harmless.
But for many marriages, the danger is quieter.
You are not throwing punches.
You are throwing looks.
You are not screaming.
You are withdrawing.
You are not leaving the house.
You are leaving emotionally.
And nobody at church knows.
Perhaps the most frightening distance between husband and wife is not measured in miles.
It is measured by how long it has been since either one felt safe enough to say:
“I miss us.”
Maybe you need to say it tonight.
Not after your spouse changes.
Not after they admit everything first.
Not after you prove who was right.
Tonight.
“I miss us.”
“I have been carrying resentment.”
“I have spoken to you with contempt.”
“I have neglected you.”
“I have used your failures against you.”
“I have stopped praying for you and started mentally prosecuting you.”
“I need Jesus to change me.”
There is something profoundly Christian about being the first person in the room to repent.
Because at the center of Christianity stands a Savior who did not wait for sinners to make themselves worthy before He loved.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8
That does not mean ignoring sin.
The cross proves precisely how serious sin is.
It means sin does not have to write the final chapter.
This is the Gospel.
We sinned against a holy God.
We could not rescue ourselves.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for sinners and rose again.
Forgiveness is not purchased by our religious performance.
Grace is not earned by pretending we have a perfect family.
We come to Christ in repentance and faith.
And the same Gospel that reconciles sinners to God begins teaching reconciled sinners how to confess, forgive, speak truth, extend mercy, and love one another.
Your marriage may have scandal in its story.
Perhaps betrayal.
Perhaps pornography.
Perhaps emotional neglect.
Perhaps financial deception.
Perhaps rage.
Perhaps years of coldness.
Perhaps words you desperately wish you could pull back into your mouth.
Perhaps you are reading this beside someone who feels a thousand miles away.
The Gospel does not call evil good.
It does something far more powerful.
It says evil does not have to have the last word.
Jesus does.
That is why our message has never been that Christians never break.
Our message is that Christ redeems broken people.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by deleting consequences.
Not by calling darkness light.
But by entering the ruins with truth, mercy, forgiveness, repentance, and resurrection power.
Peter denied Jesus.
Jesus restored Peter.
Paul persecuted the Church.
Christ transformed Paul into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
David himself committed terrible sins, and when confronted by Nathan, he eventually confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
—2 Samuel 12:13
Psalm 51 gives language to the kind of repentance every Christian eventually needs:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
—Psalm 51:10
Maybe that needs to become the prayer over your marriage.
Not first:
“God, fix my spouse.”
But:
“God, create in me a clean heart.”
Search me.
Expose me.
Correct me.
Show me where pain became bitterness.
Show me where disappointment became contempt.
Show me where leadership became control.
Show me where submission became silence before genuine wrongdoing.
Show me where correction became humiliation.
Show me where exhaustion became neglect.
Show me where I learned to perform Christianity publicly while starving my marriage privately.
Jesus, start with me.
Imagine what could happen if two people stopped competing over who had been hurt more and both fell before Christ.
Not pretending.
Not excusing.
Repenting.
Listening.
Confessing.
Forgiving.
Rebuilding.
One honest conversation at a time.
One prayer at a time.
One act of tenderness at a time.
One boundary at a time.
One changed habit at a time.
One surrendered wound at a time.
Maybe restoration will happen quickly.
Maybe it will take years.
Maybe trust has been damaged so badly that rebuilding it will require patient evidence rather than emotional promises.
Grace is free.
Trust may need to be rebuilt.
Forgiveness can be commanded by Christ.
Reconciliation ordinarily requires truth and repentance from the people involved.
Those distinctions matter.
But whatever happens next, do not allow pride to convince you that hiding is holiness.
Bring the truth into the light.
If this article exposed something you have been hiding inside your marriage, do not turn this moment into another piece of Christian content you consume and forget.
Pray.
Then act.
If appropriate and safe, go to your spouse.
Put down the phone.
Turn off the television.
Look at the person you once promised to love.
And instead of beginning with their failures, begin with your own heart.
“I need to tell you where I have been wrong.”
That sentence may be terrifying.
Say it anyway.
Not because a comment itself can heal a marriage.
Jesus is the Savior.
But there is power in finally refusing to hide.
Somebody reading silently tonight may desperately need evidence that repentance is still possible, forgiveness is still real, and God is still at work.
And if this article made you think of a husband, wife, fiancé, struggling believer, or friend whose marriage is quietly bleeding, send it to them personally.
Not as a badge announcing that your marriage is perfect.
One share can place biblical truth in front of someone we may never otherwise reach.
That is one practical way believers can use what they have to help spread truth that points people toward Christ.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
If you have been waiting for a reason to stand with this mission, let the reason be bigger than merchandise.
Let it be people.
Let it be marriages.
Let it be souls hearing about Christ.
Let it be Scripture reaching another exhausted believer at two in the morning.
Let it be another person discovering that their worst chapter does not have to become their final chapter.
Jesus Christ is still the center.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the Savior.
Jesus is the One who died.
Jesus is the One who rose.
Jesus is the One who forgives repentant sinners.
Jesus is the One who changes hearts.
Jesus is the One your marriage needs more than another argument won.
Maybe you recognized Michal in yourself.
Maybe you recognized David.
Maybe you recognized both.
Maybe you remembered the person you used to be before disappointment hardened you.
Maybe you realized that you have been looking through a window at the person you once loved and seeing only everything that went wrong.
Then perhaps tonight is not the night to decide who deserves more blame.
Perhaps tonight is the night to kneel.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
And tomorrow…
begin again.
Because sometimes the miracle is not that two people never wounded each other.
Sometimes the miracle is that Jesus met them among the wreckage, brought hidden things into the light, taught them to repent, and refused to let yesterday's sin become tomorrow's identity.
So share this with the person whose home you are praying for.
Because before a marriage can stop keeping score, somebody has to put down the ledger.
